subject: boletim
message: The text alternative "boletim" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: #paragraph-d_p_carousel_item-512337 > a > div > div > div > div > picture > img
patch.to: Ícone de documento com texto A+

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 36x36 icon (img alt="boletim") inside the 'Serviços em destaque' carousel link to /servico/consultar-boletim-escolar-digital, whose visible h2 is 'Boletim Escolar Digital'. The crop and the screenshot show a sheet with a folded corner, text lines and an 'A+' grade, which is a school report card. In Portuguese 'boletim' (as in 'boletim escolar') means report card, so the alt names exactly what the image shows. It is not a filename, a placeholder or a wrong description, so F30 does not apply. The link's visible text already gives its purpose, so the alt is at most redundant (the browser computes the link name as 'boletim Boletim Escolar Digital'). That is a best-practice point, not a 1.1.1 failure. The live page, checked 2026-10-23, still has the same image and alt. The model had a correct crop, the link text and the destination, and it judged wrongly.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 36x36 icon img (alt="boletim") inside the 'Boletim Escolar Digital' service link in the 'Serviços em destaque' carousel. The model's crop, the screenshot at the element's bounds and the live source file (a 480x557 WebP with the same filename) all show a red line icon of a sheet with an 'A+' grade, ruled lines and a folded corner: a school report card. 'Boletim' is Portuguese for a report or bulletin ('boletim escolar' = report card), so the text alternative names exactly what the image shows and the claimed mismatch does not exist. The alt is redundant with the visible heading in the same link (alt="" per H2 would be cleaner), but an accurate, redundant alternative is not a 1.1.1 failure, and it is not what the finding claims. The crop was the right image, so the model misjudged with the context it had.

ref: #paragraph-d_p_carousel-500011 > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > button:nth-of-type(2)
subject: Next
message: The icon of this button ("Next") has at most 1.61:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#cccccc on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the slick 'Next' arrow button (40x40, aria-label 'Next', no visible text) of the partner-logo carousel (Transparência, MG App, 155 LigMinas, UAI...) near the foot of the page. In the screenshot it is a #cccccc disc with the chevron cut out to the white page, on a #ffffff background: 1.61:1. The chevron against the disc gives the same 1.61:1, so neither the glyph nor its shape reaches 3:1. The live site's CSS explains it: '.paragraph--type--d-p-carousel .field--name-field-d-p-cs-item-reference .slick-arrow::before{color:#000;font-size:2.5rem;opacity:.2}', and black at 20% on white is #cccccc. Hover only raises the opacity to .3 (#b3b3b3, about 2.1:1). The theme's focus rule (opacity 1) loses to that more specific selector, so focus does not help either. The glyph is the only visual information that identifies the control. The button is not disabled (no slick-disabled class) and its look is styled by the author, so no exception applies. It fails 1.4.11 (G207 not met), as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is slick's icon-only 'Next' arrow (40x40; its 'Next' text is font-size 0 and transparent) on the partner-logo carousel. Live CSS, fetched the same day as the run, draws it as a 40px fontello circle-chevron glyph via '.paragraph--type--d-p-carousel .field--name-field-d-p-cs-item-reference .slick-arrow::before{color:#000;opacity:.2}', which renders #cccccc. The screenshot confirms a #ccc disc with a white chevron cut-out on a white page, so both disc vs page and chevron vs disc are 1.61:1. Nothing that identifies the control reaches 3:1 (G207; the Understanding text covers any visual information needed to identify that a control is present). I looked for reasons it might pass and none held up. It is not inactive: the slick init has infinite:true and there is no slick-disabled or aria-disabled. It is author-styled, not a user-agent default. Hover only raises opacity to .3 (about 2.1:1), and the same specific rule overrides slick's :focus opacity:1. The page's contrast switcher (G174) does not help: every theme uses '.theme__X *', which never matches ::before, so the glyph stays #000 at 20%, which in the hivis theme means black on black. One nuance: the carousel autoplays (autoplay:true, every 3 s), and in the full-page screenshot the UAI logo's red text touches a 6px arc of the disc, so 'at most 1.61:1' is not literally true in every frame. That contact comes from moving slide content and does not make the control identifiable, and the chevron against the disc stays at 1.61:1 in every frame.

subject: pt
message: The text alternative "pt" describes something the image does not show.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the 24px Brazilian flag inside the GTranslate language link PT in the top bar (Chrome link name 'pt PT'). In a language switcher the flag is a functional image that stands for the Portuguese language, and 'pt' names exactly that. The visible text 'PT' and the title 'Portuguese' say the same thing. 1.1.1 asks for an alternative that serves the same purpose, not a description of the flag's appearance, so the alt does not describe anything the image fails to show. At worst it repeats the adjacent text, which is a best-practice point (H2), not a 1.1.1 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The image is the 24px Brazilian flag inside the GTranslate language link (accessible name 'pt PT' from contents, title 'Portuguese', visible text 'PT', data-gt-lang='pt'). In a language switcher the flag stands for the language, and alt 'pt' names that language with the same code the visible text shows, so it serves the image's purpose. At worst it is redundant with the adjacent 'PT' (H2 would use alt=''), and redundancy is not a 1.1.1 failure. The checker judged the alt against the flag's appearance instead of its function.

The flag's purpose in the switcher is to stand for the English language, and alt 'en' names that language with the same code the visible text shows, so the alternative serves the equivalent purpose. It is merely redundant with the adjacent text, which is not a 1.1.1 failure. The finding treats the alt as a description of the picture, which is not what 1.1.1 asks of a functional image.

subject: Botão Rybená LIBRAS
message: The text alternative "Botão Rybená LIBRAS" describes something the image does not show.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the icon on the Rybená 'Voz' (text-to-speech) button in the fixed left sidebar (x 5, y 370): a speaking head with sound waves, the only visible part of the button. Its alt is 'Botão Rybená LIBRAS', copied from the sign-language button. The live rybena.js still gives all three button images this alt. The image shows nothing to do with LIBRAS (sign language). Chrome builds the button's name from its contents as 'Botão Rybená LIBRAS Voz', so screen reader users are told it is the LIBRAS button. An alternative that names the wrong function does not serve the same purpose as the image, so this fails 1.1.1 as reported.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The image is the icon of the Rybená widget's 'Voz' (text-to-speech) button: a speaking head with sound waves. Its alt is 'Botão Rybená LIBRAS', copied from the sign-language button; the live rybena.js template still gives all three buttons that alt. The image shows nothing about LIBRAS, and the alt is announced: the button's name is computed from contents as 'Botão Rybená LIBRAS Voz', and the 'Voz' label is clipped (max-width 45px, overflow hidden) until hover. The icon is neither ignorable nor given an alternative that serves its purpose, so it fails 1.1.1 as claimed. No technique or context rescues it.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The image is the eye icon of the Rybená '+ Acessibilidade' (visual tools, class btn-rybena-vision) button. The image shows nothing about LIBRAS, and the alt is part of the announced name 'Botão Rybená LIBRAS + Acessibilidade', while the visible label is clipped until hover. The text alternative misidentifies the control's function, so it does not serve the equivalent purpose; this is a real 1.1.1 failure.

subject: Registre sua manifestação
message: The link text "Registre sua manifestação" is shared by 5 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.

patch.ref: #main > div > section > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > section > div > div > div > section > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > h3 > a
patch.after: Registre sua manifestação (Ouvidoria)

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the h3 link 'Registre sua manifestação' of the green Destaques card, which goes to the general Ouvidoria form (index.jsf). The next card has an h3 link and an icon link with the same name that go to index.jsf?canalAtendimento=D, which the live form shows as the 'Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher' channel. Sighted users tell the two cards apart only by their SVG icons ('Ouvidoria Nacional de Justiça' vs 'Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher'). Those icons are drawn as paths with no text alternative, and the icon links carry aria-label 'Registre sua manifestação'. So the two links have the same text and identical programmatic context (the h3 and the card), but their destinations are not equivalent. The ACT rule for 2.4.4 (fd3a94) counts identical names in identical contexts as a failure. The claim holds.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the heading link 'Registre sua manifestação' of the second 'Destaques' card. That card's icon reads 'Ouvidoria Nacional de Justiça – Formulário Eletrônico' and the link goes to the general CNJ Ouvidoria form (index.jsf). The third card has identical heading and icon names but goes to index.jsf?canalAtendimento=D, which I confirmed opens the 'Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher' form. The text that tells the cards apart exists only as SVG paths inside an aria-labelled sibling link, so nothing programmatic distinguishes this link, as claimed. But its own text accurately describes its destination, the page's general form, which the sidebar link with the same text also reaches. Understanding 2.4.4 calls distinct text for distinct destinations a best practice, and the under-described links are the women's-ombudsman ones. Competent auditors could fail this link as half of an indistinguishable pair or pass it.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the icon link of the purple Destaques card. It has tabindex=-1, but it is in the accessibility tree and reachable in browse mode and link lists. It carries aria-label 'Registre sua manifestação' and goes to index.jsf?canalAtendimento=D, the Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher form (checked on the live form). Its visible content is an SVG reading 'Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher / Formulário Eletrônico'. The aria-label replaces that with a name shared by four other links, three of which go to the general form. Nothing programmatic conveys that this link is the women's ombudsman channel, so its purpose cannot be determined, as the finding says. This fails 2.4.4, and the name mismatch is also a 2.5.3 issue.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the icon link of the third 'Destaques' card (tabindex -1, but still exposed to screen readers). Its image reads 'Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher – Formulário Eletrônico', but aria-label 'Registre sua manifestação' replaces that. It leads to index.jsf?canalAtendimento=D, which I confirmed opens the Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher form, while links with the same name go to the general form (index.jsf). 'Mulher' exists only as vector paths; the only SVG text is 'Formulário Eletrônico', which the general card shows too. So nothing programmatic reveals this link's distinct purpose, and the context sighted users get is not made available as Understanding 2.4.4 requires. (The image text missing from the name is also a 2.5.3 issue.)

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the h3 link 'Registre sua manifestação' of the purple card, which goes to the Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher form (canalAtendimento=D; the live form shows that heading). It has the same text as the general-form links in the sidebar and in the green card, and its context (h3, card) is identical to theirs. A screen reader user cannot tell that this link is the women's channel, while sighted users can, so this fails 2.4.4 as reported (ACT rule fd3a94).

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the heading link 'Registre sua manifestação' of the third 'Destaques' card. It leads to index.jsf?canalAtendimento=D, which I confirmed is the Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher form, while the identical heading link in the second card and the sidebar link go to the general form. The only thing that says 'Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher' is vector art in the sibling icon link, whose name is also 'Registre sua manifestação'. No text or programmatic context tells this link apart, so a screen-reader user cannot tell it reaches the women's ombudsman. That fails 2.4.4 as claimed; the live page is unchanged.

subject: www.cnj.jus.br/comopeticionar.
message: The link text "www.cnj.jus.br/comopeticionar." is an address, not a purpose.

patch.ref: #main > div > section > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > section > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > p:nth-of-type(13) > a
patch.after: Como acionar o CNJ

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The link text is the URL 'www.cnj.jus.br/comopeticionar.' at the end of the sentence 'As demandas que sejam da competência do Plenário ou da Corregedoria Nacional de Justiça devem ser promovidas e encaminhadas de acordo com o Regimento Interno do CNJ, conforme orientações previstas na página …'. That enclosing sentence is programmatically determined context (G53), and it states the purpose: the page with guidance on filing such demands. The link does lead to 'Como acionar o CNJ', and the URL ('como peticionar', how to petition) is meaningful too. 2.4.4 does not forbid a URL as link text when the context gives the purpose, so this passes. The finding applies a stricter 'an address is not a purpose' rule.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The link text is the address 'www.cnj.jus.br/comopeticionar.' at the end of the sentence 'As demandas ... devem ser promovidas e encaminhadas de acordo com o Regimento Interno do CNJ, conforme orientações previstas na página www.cnj.jus.br/comopeticionar.' That enclosing sentence is its programmatically determined context, and it states the purpose: the page with guidance on how to petition the CNJ (G53). The destination is 'Como acionar o CNJ', and the address itself (como peticionar) redirects there. 2.4.4 does not forbid an address as link text when the context gives the purpose, so the checker applied a stricter rule than the criterion.

subject: Início
message: The link text "Início" is shared by 4 links that lead to 4 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.

patch.after: Página inicial da UFPE

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: 'Início' (/inicio) is an entry of #search-list, the page-suggestion dropdown (ul.dropdown-menu) under the header search field. On the live page (checked the same day, markup unchanged) that list is display:none (Bootstrap .dropdown-menu rule in the theme's aui.css) until the user types two or more characters, and an inline script then shows only the entries whose name contains the query; Rampa's capture rendered the page without its theme stylesheet (default Times New Roman, the list about 59,000 px tall in the screenshot), so every entry looked like a visible link. The others are the home pages of other sites in the same list: /ppgci/incio, /df/inicio and /biomedicina-bacharelado-cb/inicio (the live list has 8 such entries). When the dropdown shows such entries together, nothing on the page, visual or programmatic, tells them apart for anyone (same text, same title attribute, no unit name), so their purpose is ambiguous to users in general and the 2.4.4 exception applies (Understanding 2.4.4; ACT rule fd3a94 background): different text for different destinations is a best practice, not a 2.4.4 requirement.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The link 'Início' (href /inicio) is reported as sharing its text with links to other places. It is item 2 of ul#search-list, the search box's type-ahead suggestion dropdown (class dropdown-menu): on the live page aui.css hides it (.aui .dropdown-menu{display:none}) and the inline filter() script shows it only after two or more characters are typed, and then only the items whose name contains the query. Rampa captured the page with the theme CSS unapplied (the screenshot is unstyled HTML, even the sr-only skip links show), so 1,628 of its 3,302 items appeared as an always-visible list of links. The four 'Início' links in the snapshot go to /inicio (the UFPE home page), /ppgci/incio (302 to the PPGCI site), /df/inicio and /biomedicina-bacharelado-cb/inicio (302 to that course's site); I checked them on the live site, and the full list has eight. When the dropdown does show these items they look identical (same text, same chevron icon, no grouping or heading), so sighted users cannot tell them apart either. That is the 2.4.4 exception for purposes ambiguous to users in general: Understanding 2.4.4 says the person with a disability is not at a disadvantage when the page offers no context. ACT rule fd3a94 passes such pairs when there is no visual information that tells them apart, and it treats separate list items as different contexts. Different text for different destinations is only a best practice there.

subject: unmarked|pt-BR|(Poscivil) Graduate Program in
message: This passage has no lang attribute, so it is read as Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR), but it is in English (en).

patch.after: (Poscivil) Graduate Program in

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the list item '(Poscivil) Graduate Program in Civil Engineering' (link to /poscivil) in the header search field's suggestion dropdown (#search-list). Its text is English and neither it nor any ancestor has a lang attribute, so it inherits the page's lang='pt-BR'; the live page still has this entry, with no lang anywhere inside the list. The dropdown is hidden until a matching query is typed (for example 'civil' or 'pr'), but then the entry is shown and exposed, so it is content in that state. It is not a language-neutral proper name: it is an English translation of the program's name (its own page's heading is 'Programa de Pós-Graduação em Engenharia Civil (Poscivil)'), while the Understanding document describes proper names as names used across languages without translation. A pt-BR voice would mispronounce it, and marking it lang='en' (H58) is what 3.1.2 asks, so this is a real 3.1.2 failure.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is item 626 of ul#search-list, the search box's type-ahead suggestion dropdown: the text '(Poscivil) Graduate Program in Civil Engineering', linking to /poscivil. Neither the li nor the link has a lang attribute and the page is lang=pt-BR, so a screen reader would read the English words with Portuguese rules when the item is shown. On the live page the dropdown is hidden (.aui .dropdown-menu{display:none}) and shows this item only once a matching query such as 'civil' is typed; Rampa captured it unstyled, as always-visible text. The bigger doubt is the exception for proper names. The text is the program's own name (the /poscivil site is titled '(Poscivil) Graduate Program in Civil Engineering - UFPE'), and Understanding 3.1.2 says proper names generally need no change of language, naming specific entities 'including, but not limited to' brands, people and places. Against that, the text is a translated title made of ordinary English words. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether an English program name counts as a proper name, so I cannot call it either way.

subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the image link (a.svg-anchor, data-asoch-targets ochImage) of a Google responsive display ad (Jeep Avenger) in the iframe 'Publicidade', inside an anchor container fixed to the bottom of the viewport. Its only content is an empty SVG painted with a CSS background image: no title, no aria-label, empty SVG hash, and the SVG is ignored in the accessibility tree. Chrome's accessibility tree lists the anchor as a focusable link with no name and no name source. An image as the only content of a link with no accessible name is the documented failure F89 of 4.1.2. The ad is third-party and rotates: the full-page screenshot does not show the fixed ad, and the live page may serve a different creative. At capture time, though, this unnamed link was on the page. Third-party status matters only for a conformance claim.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the image link (data-asoch-targets 'ad0,ochImage') in the Google Jeep Avenger ad. The ad sits in a fixed bottom banner and is visible in the screenshot. The link's only content is an empty SVG painted with a CSS background image, with no title, aria-label or text. Chrome's accessibility tree exposes it as a focusable link with no name and no name source, and the snapshot also computes none. The iframe's 'Publicidade' label names the frame, not the link. The headline link next to it goes to the same place, but a duplicate named link does not give this one a name, and no aria-hidden hides it. This matches F89 (an image as the only content of a link, with no accessible name), which WCAG lists as a 4.1.2 failure. The ad is third-party content, but it is presented on the page, and WCAG allows only a partial-conformance statement for that, not an exemption. Ads rotate, so the live page may now show a different ad.

Its only content is an empty SVG with a CSS background image of the advertiser logo, with no title, aria-label or text. The SVG is ignored in the accessibility tree, and Chrome exposes the anchor as a focusable link with no computed name. That fails 4.1.2 (F89). Other links in the ad with the same href have names ('Jeep Avenger: Confira Versões', 'Abrir'), but that does not name this one. The ad is third-party and rotating, so the live page may differ, but the failure was real on the captured page.

skeptic.label: true_positive

Like the image link, it holds only an empty SVG with a CSS background image. This is the F89 pattern and a real 4.1.2 failure of content shown on the page, although the content is third-party. The ad seen at collection time may no longer be served live.

subject: Image
message: The text alternative "Image" is a placeholder, not a description: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The footer image cartoes.jpg sits under the address paragraph. The screenshot shows a strip of accepted payment methods (Visa, Mastercard, Elo, Amex, Diners, Aura, Hipercard, Discover, JCB, Hiper, Pix), and no nearby text lists them, so the image is informative. Chrome exposes it as an image named "Image" (name from alt), so a screen reader reads a placeholder that describes nothing (F30). If it were treated as decorative, a non-null alt like "Image" would still fail (F39). The live HTML still has alt="Image".

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the footer image cartoes.jpg. The screenshot shows it rendered as a row of payment brand logos (Visa, Mastercard, Elo, Amex, Diners, Aura, Hipercard, Discover, JCB, Hiper, Pix), and no text on the page lists the accepted payment methods. Its alt is "Image", which is the same in the live HTML and is what the accessibility tree exposes as its name. Placeholder text like "image" is a documented 1.1.1 failure (F30). Even if the image were treated as decorative, a non-null alt such as "image" still fails (F39). The snapshot's null bounds and skipped image analysis are collector gaps that do not matter here, because the alt is in the DOM and the image is visibly rendered. No way for it to pass holds up.

message: The field "Nome" asks for the user's full name but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="name" is missing.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the text input with the placeholder "Nome" in the newsletter sign-up ("Receba nossas novidades e sugestões"). It collects the subscriber's own name, a purpose on the WCAG Input Purposes list. Neither the snapshot nor the live HTML has an autocomplete attribute, and the ASP.NET name "wctnewsletter1$txtnome" is not a programmatic purpose. H98 is not met and the purpose cannot be determined, so the field fails 1.3.5. That would hold even if "given-name" were the better token than "name".

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the "Nome" field of the newsletter sign-up ("Receba nossas novidades e sugestões"), labelled only by its placeholder. It collects the subscriber's own name. Neither the snapshot (taken after scripts ran) nor the live HTML gives it an autocomplete attribute, and nothing else identifies its purpose. A name is a listed input purpose and HTML supports autocomplete, so the purpose is not programmatically determinable. Its validator accepts one or more words, so name (or given-name) would be the right token; either way the missing purpose is the real 1.3.5 failure the finding describes. I found no context or technique that makes it pass.

The site's bootstrap-iso.css sets the placeholder color to rgba(0,0,0,0.2) with !important, and the field has an inline white background. The field is enabled, so the inactive-component exception does not apply, and the placeholder is not a logotype or decoration. The measurement is confirmed and no exception holds, so this is a real failure.

subject: Fale conosco pelo WhatsApp
message: The icon of this link ("Fale conosco pelo WhatsApp") has at most 1.98:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #25d366). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
html: <a href="https://wa.me/5521998812782?text=Ol%C3%A1." class="floatWP" target="_blank" rel="noopener" aria-label="Fale conosco pelo WhatsApp">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the fixed floating link to wa.me: a 56px #25d366 disc holding the white FontAwesome WhatsApp glyph. The 1.98:1 figure is right, and the disc against the white page is also about 2:1. But the glyph is the WhatsApp logo shown in WhatsApp's own colors, the white mark on WhatsApp green of its app icon. Understanding 1.4.11 lists logos under the essential exception. It also says that when a logo is the only content of a control, the exemption "carries over" to that control normatively, and that a higher-contrast variant is only a recommended practice. The low contrast comes from the brand, not from an author dimming a logo that normally has good contrast. So this is not a 1.4.11 failure, and the G207 icon rule was applied to a brand logo. The control's focus indicator would still be in scope, but this finding is not about it.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the floating WhatsApp link: the Font Awesome WhatsApp brand glyph, in white on a #25d366 circle. The screenshot confirms 1.98:1 between glyph and circle, so the measurement is right. But the icon is the WhatsApp logo in WhatsApp's own brand colours (#25D366 green with white), and WhatsApp's brand guidelines say not to modify the colours of its logos. The Understanding document for 1.4.11 exempts logos from contrast requirements. For logos that act as links or other controls, it calls a higher-contrast variant only a best practice. It denies the exemption only when the author lowers a logo's normal contrast, which is not the case here, since the WhatsApp mark's normal presentation has this contrast. So the claim that 1.4.11 requires 3:1 here applies a stricter rule than WCAG's documented interpretation. An auditor reading only the normative UI-component clause might still fail it, but the WCAG guidance supports a pass.

subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <a class="icon busca-bar" onclick="clickBuscaRefinada();" style="background-image: url(images/search.svg);content: '';height: 25px;width: 25px;display: inline-block;	background-repeat: no-repeat;	background-size: 100% 100%;" "="">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The magnifying glass beside the header search field is <a class="icon busca-bar" onclick="clickBuscaRefinada();">. Its icon is a CSS background image, and it has no text, aria-label, title or href. Chrome's accessibility tree (CDP) exposes it as a link, because Chrome maps anchors with click listeners to link, and its name is empty. A screen reader announces only "link" for a control that runs the search. A UI component with no name fails 4.1.2, as the finding says. The live HTML is unchanged. With no href or tabindex it is probably not in the tab order either, which is a separate 2.1.1 concern.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the magnifier icon next to the header search box. It is an <a> with no href, text, title or ARIA attributes, drawn with a CSS background image, and its onclick (clickBuscaRefinada) runs the site search. The live HTML is unchanged. Chrome's accessibility tree, captured through CDP in the snapshot, exposes it as a link with no name, so the finding's claim is accurate. It is a scripted user interface control with no programmatically determined name, which F68 documents as a 4.1.2 failure, and nothing on the page supplies a name. Without an href or tabindex it is probably not keyboard reachable either, but that is a separate 2.1.1 issue and does not affect this one.

subject: Digite aqui o que você procura
message: The placeholder "Digite aqui o que você procura" has a contrast of 2.32:1 with the field (#aaaaaa on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input type="search" class="form-control busca-texto txtBuscaProd" id="txtBuscaProd" name="txtBuscaProd" placeholder="Digite aqui o que você procura" aria-label="Campo de busca" autocomplete="off" onclick="ObterTermosMaisBuscados(this, event)" tabindex="0">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the header search field (#txtBuscaProd). Its placeholder, "Digite aqui o que você procura", is styled by the site's own rule .form-control::placeholder{color:#aaa} on a white field, at 15px and weight 400. I checked the live CSS and it is unchanged. The darkest glyph pixels in the screenshot are #aaaaaa on #ffffff, which gives 2.32:1, far below the 4.5:1 that normal-size text needs. Placeholder text is visible text and is not incidental. Here it is also the only visible text that says what the field is for, because the label is hidden. The W3C WAI forms tutorial treats placeholder text as subject to the minimum contrast requirement. This is a real 1.4.3 failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header search field #txtBuscaProd. Its placeholder "Digite aqui o que você procura" is the only visible text on the field, which has no visible label. I checked whether the measurement could be an artefact or a default colour. The site's own CSS sets .form-control{font-size:15px} and .form-control::placeholder{color:#aaa} (overriding Bootstrap's darker default), and the screenshot's glyph cores are exactly #aaaaaa on #ffffff, which is 2.32:1. The 1.4.3 Understanding document says the criterion applies to placeholder text. At 15px and weight 400 the text is not large, so 4.5:1 applies, and 2.32:1 would fail even the 3:1 large-text threshold. None of the exceptions applies (the field is active, the text is not decorative and is not a logo). The live page still has the same CSS.

subject: Buscar
message: The icon of this button ("Buscar") has at most 2.46:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #ff8400). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
html: <button class="btn btn-orange-ka px-3 py-2 rounded-end" id="btnPesquisa" type="button" aria-label="Buscar" title="Buscar" onclick="ObterProdutosPorTermoBuscado(document.getElementById('txtBuscaProd'), event, true)" tabindex="0">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the icon-only search button (#btnPesquisa, aria-label "Buscar"). All it shows is a magnifier SVG with fill #fff on the .btn-orange-ka background #ff8400. I checked the live CSS and sampled the screenshot: the pixels are #ffffff on #ff8400, which gives 2.46:1, and hover keeps the same colours. The magnifier is the only visual sign of what the button does, so it is a graphical object required for understanding. G207, including its example of a white icon inside a coloured shape, measures the icon against that adjacent colour and asks for 3:1. The orange box stands out against the black header at about 8.5:1, but that does not make the icon itself perceivable. This is a real 1.4.11 failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is #btnPesquisa, the search submit button. It has no visible text: its aria-label and title are "Buscar", and a white SVG magnifier (.componentheader__icon--white{fill:#fff}) sits on .btn-orange-ka, whose background is #ff8400 (also #ff8400 on hover). The screenshot pixels confirm #ffffff on #ff8400, which is 2.46:1. I looked for a reason it could pass. The orange box contrasts about 8.5:1 with the black header, so the control's presence is visible, but the magnifier is the only thing that shows what the button does. The 1.4.11 Understanding document counts a stand-alone icon with no text as a graphical object, and its Figure 17 measures a white icon against its orange shape, needing 3:1. Its allowance for position or context concerns showing that something is a button, not the icon that labels it, and the title tooltip appears only on hover. The icon falls short of 3:1 against the only colour next to it.

subject:  Comprar Agora
message: The link text " Comprar Agora" is shared by 2 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.

patch.before:  Comprar Agora
patch.after: Comprar Plástico para Plastificação A4

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the "Comprar Agora" link in carousel slide 3 (an li with role=tabpanel named "3 of 21", inside a ul with role=presentation). Its onclick, Comprar('629951'), adds product 629951 to the basket, and its href goes to that product's page. The other visible slide has an identical "Comprar Agora" link for a different product (608683). The hidden slides are aria-hidden, so these two are the only ones exposed, which matches the message. The product name is just above the link, in a separate name-and-price link in the same slide. So the link is told apart visually and in reading order, but not by programmatically determined link context. The name is not in the same sentence, paragraph or table cell. role=tabpanel replaces the li's list-item semantics, and the link's nearest block container holds only the link. The slide's name says nothing about the product, and there is no aria-label, aria-labelledby or aria-describedby. Both checks of F63's test procedure fail. The live page has the same markup. The message goes too far in saying that nothing around the link tells it apart, since the card does visually, but the 2.4.4 failure it names holds.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale:
The element is the "Comprar Agora" link in carousel slide 3. Its href goes to the page of product 629951 (plastic laminating pouches), and its onclick Comprar('629951') adds that product to the basket. Slide 4 has an identical link for another product, and at snapshot time these were the only two such links not aria-hidden, so they share one text with different purposes. I looked for programmatically determined context that would name the product. The link sits alone in div.d-block. The product name is a

inside a separate link before it. The link has no aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-describedby or title, and no heading names the product (the preceding heading is the h1 "Apresentação", and H80 is only advisory in WCAG 2.2). The card's li is not usable as list-item context: Splide gives it role=tabpanel with aria-label "3 of 21" and makes the ul role=presentation, and H77 also requires the li to be the nearest block-level ancestor, which it is not. This matches F63: the context is only in an adjacent element, so the user must leave the link to find it. The product name appearing next to the link on screen does not count, and the live markup is unchanged.

subject:  Comprar Agora
message: The link text " Comprar Agora" is shared by 2 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.

patch.before:  Comprar Agora
patch.after: Comprar Projetor Multimídia Intelbras PFL5211

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the "Comprar Agora" link in carousel slide 4 (an li with role=tabpanel named "4 of 21", inside a ul with role=presentation). Its onclick, Comprar('608683'), adds product 608683 to the basket, and its href goes to that product's page. The other visible slide has an identical "Comprar Agora" link for a different product (629951). The hidden slides are aria-hidden, so these two are the only ones exposed, which matches the message. The product name is just above the link, in a separate name-and-price link in the same slide. So the link is told apart visually and in reading order, but not by programmatically determined link context. The name is not in the same sentence, paragraph or table cell. role=tabpanel replaces the li's list-item semantics, and the link's nearest block container holds only the link. The slide's name says nothing about the product, and there is no aria-label, aria-labelledby or aria-describedby. Both checks of F63's test procedure fail. The live page has the same markup. The message goes too far in saying that nothing around the link tells it apart, since the card does visually, but the 2.4.4 failure it names holds.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the "Comprar Agora" link in carousel slide 4. Its href goes to the page of product 608683 (an Intelbras 5200-lumen projector), and its onclick Comprar('608683') adds that product to the basket. Its text is identical to slide 3's link for a different product, and those were the only two exposed at snapshot time. The structure is the same as slide 3, so the same checks apply. The link is alone in div.d-block, and the product name and price sit in a separate preceding link. There is no ARIA name, description or title, and no heading names the product. The li is changed to a tabpanel labelled "4 of 21" inside a presentation ul, so it provides no list-item context, and it is not the nearest block-level ancestor that H77 requires. The surrounding text is therefore not programmatically determined link context (F63), and the link text alone does not say which product it buys. Visual proximity does not satisfy 2.4.4, and the live markup is unchanged.

ref: #__next > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > picture > img
subject: Logo IC Cultural
message: The text alternative "Logo IC Cultural" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

patch.ref: #__next > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > picture > img

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the site logo in the header (it shows the mark and the word 'ItaúCultural'). It is the only content of a link to '/' and has alt 'Logo IC Cultural'. The live page is unchanged. When a linked site logo has a text alternative that names the organization, that is the usual, accepted pattern for a home link. Sighted users get the same cue: a logo that, by convention, leads home. So the alternative serves the equivalent purpose, and no documented 1.1.1 failure applies (not F30, F39 or F89). Adding 'página inicial', as in the WAI tutorial's 'W3C home', is best practice, not a 1.1.1 requirement. The alt has other flaws: the extra word 'Logo', and 'IC Cultural' where the logo reads 'Itaú Cultural'. The finding does not claim either one, and the alt still identifies the organization.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header logo (a picture whose desktop source is the full \C ItaúCultural wordmark) and it is the only content of a link to "/". Its alt is "Logo IC Cultural", which becomes the link's whole accessible name. That matches the live page. The finding's factual claim holds: the name describes the image as a logo and never says "home". WAI's functional-images tutorial recommends "Example.com homepage" rather than "Example.com logo", and H30 says a link's only image should describe the link's function, so a strict auditor would fail it. The counter-argument is concrete, though. The alt names the organisation, a header logo linking to the site's home page is a universal convention, and a sighted user gets no more from the image than that, so the alt can be read as serving the equivalent purpose. WCAG's normative text and documented 1.1.1 failures (F30, F38, F65 and so on) do not cover this case. Competent auditors split on this exact pattern (many would call it best practice, or a 2.4.4 matter), so I cannot settle it either way.

patch.ref: #__next > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > picture > img
patch.to: Banner da série Ocupação em vídeos com nomes de artistas brasileiros e botão 'Saber mais'.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 1280x450 banner image of the 'Ocupação em vídeos' promo. Its desktop source is ocupacaoConteudoDesk.png: a black field with a collage of the names of artists honored by the Ocupação series. The heading, paragraph and 'Saber mais' link over it are HTML text, not part of the image. Its alt is 'image banner', in the snapshot and on the live page. Screen readers announce that alt, but it conveys nothing. If the image is treated as decorative, it should have alt="", and a non-null alt like 'image' is failure F39. If it is treated as informative, the alt must convey its content, and placeholder text is failure F30. Either way, 'image banner' fails 1.1.1, so the finding's claim holds.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 1280x450 banner img inside the "Ocupação em vídeos" promo. Its picture source with no media query serves ocupacaoConteudoDesk.png, a black field covered with orange names of artists honoured in the series. The heading, paragraph and "Saber mais" link are real HTML laid over it. The img has alt="image banner" and the accessibility tree exposes it as an image with that name, with no aria-hidden or presentation role. The live markup is unchanged. I looked for a way it could pass and found none. If the image is informative (it names the honourees), "image banner" is placeholder text that is not an alternative (F30). If it is treated as decorative backdrop, a non-null alt keeps it from being ignored by assistive technology (F38). Either way 1.1.1 fails, and the finding's claim that the alt is a generic non-description names that failure. In the decorative reading the right fix would be alt="" rather than a longer description.

subject: #__next > a
message: The icon of this link has at most 1.99:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #61ce70). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the fixed floating link to wa.me: a 56 px circle in #61ce70 holding a white WhatsApp glyph, with no text. It also has no accessible name, which is a separate 4.1.2/2.4.4 issue. The measurement is right: the site CSS confirms white on #61ce70, which is 1.99:1. But the glyph is the WhatsApp brand logo, shown in the brand's own white-on-green presentation. Understanding 1.4.11 exempts logos under the essential exception. It also says the exemption normatively carries over to a control whose only visible content is the logo; using a higher-contrast variant is only a recommendation. The site's green is not WhatsApp's #25D366, but #25D366 with white gives the same 1.98:1. So the low contrast comes from the brand palette, not from an author choice that would void the exemption. This is a best-practice concern, not a 1.4.11 failure: the rule applied G207's icon test without the logo exception.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the fixed WhatsApp floating link. The CSS gives .floating-button a background of #61ce70, the SVG path has fill #fff, and the screenshot pixels confirm #ffffff on #61ce70, so the measured 1.99:1 is right. The graphic, though, is the WhatsApp brand logo: the speech bubble with a phone, white on green. Understanding 1.4.11 exempts logos and logotypes under the essential exception. It says that when a logo is the only visible content of a user interface component, the exemption normatively carries over to that component, and a higher-contrast variant is only a recommended practice. The author-choice caveat applies when a logo that normally has enough contrast is presented with less. That is not the case here: WhatsApp's approved pairings (white on #25D366, or green on white) measure 1.98:1, the same as this button, so the low contrast comes from the brand design, not from the site's slightly different green. The rule applied G207's icon requirement without the logo exception. The link does have a real problem, since it has no accessible name (2.4.4/4.1.2, F89), but that is a different criterion.

message: Nothing on screen tells what to enter in the field "Buscar": its label is on the page, but its text does not show: the label looks the same with its text made transparent.

patch.after: <label for="searchDesk">Buscar</label> <input id="searchDesk" type="search" name="searchDesk" aria-labelledby="searchDesk">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the desktop header search input (#searchDesk). At capture it sat in a collapsed form (width 0, overflow hidden, right -30%) past the 1280 px viewport edge, which is why the crop the model saw is blank. The site's live JS and CSS, which match the snapshot, show what happens when the user clicks the header magnifier icon. The form gets the class 'active' and widens to a 600 px white field, and the input takes focus. The field shows a 40 px magnifier icon at its left (a background image, bloom.svg) and a close X at its right. The 'Buscar' label is indeed hidden behind the input (z-index -1), and there is no placeholder. But Understanding 3.3.2 describes this exact case: a global search field in the header whose loupe icon serves as its visible label. It also says image labels meet the criterion. So the field has a label whenever it is shown. The checker never saw the field open. A keyboard user can tab into the hidden, collapsed input, but that is a focus-visibility issue (2.4.7), not a 3.3.2 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: #searchDesk is the header search field. On desktop its form.accessibility-search is collapsed (width:0, right:-30%, overflow:hidden) and only opens to 600px with .active, when the user clicks the magnifier toggle in the header. When Rampa collected the page, the form, label and input all sat beyond the 1280px viewport (x 1302 to 1462). The crop the model saw is blank white, and the test that made the label text transparent compared pixels that were never on screen. In the open state the label is still hidden behind the input (position:absolute; z-index:-1). However, the input's CSS paints a magnifying-glass icon (bloom.svg) at its left edge, and the user reached the field through a magnifier button. Understanding 3.3.2 names exactly this case: a global header search field paired with a loupe icon, which serves as its visible label and needs no instructions. It also says images can serve as labels. So something on screen does tell the user what the field is for, and the claim that nothing does is an artefact of collecting the field while it was collapsed off-screen. The field is focusable while invisible, which is a focus-visibility concern (2.4.7), not 3.3.2.

subject: Home - Canada.ca
message: The page title "Home - Canada.ca" says nothing about this page.

patch.after: <title>Government of Canada - Official Website</title>

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The finding is about the document title of the Canada.ca English home page. The title is "Home - Canada.ca" in the snapshot, and still was on the live page when I checked it on 2026-10-23. The page is the site's landing page. The screenshot shows the H1 "Canada.ca" with the tagline "The official website of the Government of Canada", then "Most requested" tasks, "Services and information" and "Your government". A title made of "Home" plus the site name states exactly that purpose. It also tells this page apart from the rest of the site, whose pages are titled "<topic> - Canada.ca" ("Jobs - Canada.ca", "Benefits - Canada.ca" and so on, in the destinations Rampa read). The only other destination with the same title is the basic-HTML version of this same page (?wbdisable=true). The title is not empty, placeholder text, a filename or a title shared by every page, so F25 does not apply, and it passes G88's checks (relevant to the content, identifies the page). The 2.4.2 Understanding document's own landing-page example is titled with the site's name. The page meets 2.4.2. Rampa had the title, URL, H1 and page content and judged wrongly that the title says nothing about the page, in effect asking a home page's title for more than the criterion requires.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The finding is about the document title of the Canada.ca home page. The snapshot and the live page (fetched 2026-10-23, unchanged) both have the title "Home - Canada.ca". The page's h1 is "Canada.ca", its tagline is "The official website of the Government of Canada", and the page is the site's home portal to government services. So the title says exactly what the page is: the home page of the Canada.ca site. That meets 2.4.2. The Understanding document's own example titles a landing page with just the site name ("ARIA Authoring Practices Guide | APG | WAI | W3C"), and G88 example 4 titles a front page "National News, Front Page". None of F25's failure conditions applies: it is not a default or placeholder title, a filename, or empty, and it is not one template title reused on every page, since inner pages have their own titles ("Jobs - Canada.ca", "Taxes - Canada.ca", "About government - Canada.ca"). The checker had the title, the h1 and the page text, and still judged that the title says nothing about the page. That is a wrong judgment, and in effect it asks for more than WCAG requires.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Card image 'Three people outdoors with Edinburgh Castle in the background.' linking to https://study.ed.ac.uk/ (the 'Study with us' card). The img is the only content of a focusable <a> (the accessible name comes from contents and equals the alt; there is no aria-hidden and no tabindex=-1, in the snapshot and on the live page). The alt describes the photo, not where the link goes. Understanding 1.1.1 puts linked images under Situation C (controls) with H30: 'When an image is the only content of a link, the text alternative for the image describes the unique function of the link'. The WAI functional-images tutorial says the same, and the Understanding examples use the destination ('Smallville Times', 'International Travel'). The heading link to the same URL right after it does not give the image link a name that describes its purpose: it only makes it a redundant link (H2 would merge the two, or the image link could be hidden from assistive technology). This is a real, if low-impact, 1.1.1 failure; 2.4.4 also applies.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The img is the only content of a focusable, exposed link (no aria-hidden or tabindex), so its alt "Three people outdoors with Edinburgh Castle in the background." is the link's whole accessible name; the link goes to https://study.ed.ac.uk/ ("Study with us"), the same href as the card heading link right after it. H30 (sufficient for 1.1.1) requires the alt of an image-only link to describe the link's purpose, and this alt describes the photo instead. Nothing in it points to studying at Edinburgh. The redundant heading link does not give this link a name, and the live page is unchanged. The claim holds.

It is the illustrative photo of the 'Research and teaching' card (a student taking a book from library shelves), directly above the h3 'Research and teaching' (the live page is the same). The check required a literal description of the scene, which is more than 1.1.1's equivalent-purpose test asks.

WCAG does not require a literal description of an illustrative card photo. At most, alt="" would avoid repeating the heading, which is redundancy and not the mismatch the finding claims. The model passed the same pattern on the Visit, About us and Open Days cards.

subject: Pimoroni
message: The text alternative "Pimoroni" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the PIMORONI wordmark (svg role="img" aria-label="Pimoroni"), the only content of the header link to "/". The text alternative matches the wordmark word for word, and a logo that links to the site's home page is a convention users know, so "Pimoroni" gives screen reader users what sighted users get. The link also has title="Back to the home page", which Chrome exposes as its accessible description (the snapshot's CDP node has name "Pimoroni" and description "Back to the home page"), so the destination is available programmatically. Adding "home" to the alt is best practice from the WAI images tutorial, not a 1.1.1 requirement, and no documented failure covers a home logo link whose alt is the organisation's name. The live page has the same markup.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the PIMORONI wordmark SVG (role=img, aria-label="Pimoroni"). It is the only rendered content of the header logo link to "/", and on this page that link points back to the page itself. The text alternative matches the wordmark's text and names the site the link goes to. WCAG 1.1.1 does not require a linked logo's alternative to add "home": the WAI tutorial's "W3C home" is advisory, and no failure technique covers this. The link also has title="Back to the home page", which Chrome exposes as its accessible description (the snapshot's ax data shows it), so the destination is announced anyway. Requiring the alt text itself to state the destination is stricter than the criterion.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the product photo of the Sonoff AirGuard e-ink sensor in the first 'Just landed' card. Its alt is "Default Title", Shopify's placeholder title for a product's only variant; the tile script on the live page still builds the alt from the variant title (alt="${hit.title}"). That text describes nothing in the image, and it is announced: the browser's accessible name for the card link is "Default Title New Sonoff AirGuard E-Ink Zigbee Temperature and Humidity Sensor". The photo could have been given alt="" because the product name sits next to it in the link, but a placeholder or programming reference used as the alternative is documented failure F30, so 1.1.1 fails as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the product photo in the first 'Just landed' card (the Sonoff AirGuard sensor). The snapshot shows alt="Default Title", and Chrome puts it into the card link's name ("Default Title New Sonoff AirGuard..."). That is Shopify's placeholder variant title: the live theme script still builds the alt from the variant title. It does not describe the photo, and it is not the empty alt that would let assistive technology skip an image that repeats the product name. Placeholder text used as a text alternative is the documented failure F30. I looked for a reason it could pass: it is not a collector artefact, and treating the image as decorative does not help, because the junk name is still announced. None held up.

message: The field "Enter your e-mail address" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.

patch.before: <input type="email" value="" name="EMAIL" class="required email" id="mce-EMAIL" placeholder="Enter your e-mail address">
patch.after: <input type="email" value="" name="EMAIL" class="required email" id="mce-EMAIL" placeholder="Enter your e-mail address" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the footer newsletter field (#mce-EMAIL, type="email", name="EMAIL"). The text beside it offers news 'delivered directly to your inbox', so it asks for the user's own address, which is information about the user, and 'email' is one of the listed input purposes. The field has no autocomplete attribute, both in the snapshot and on the live page today. type="email" gives only the data type, which the Understanding document says does not identify the purpose. Chrome's autofill check (FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError) flags the field too. Without autocomplete="email" (H98), 1.3.5 fails.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The field is the footer newsletter input (type=email, id mce-EMAIL, placeholder "Enter your e-mail address"). It asks for the visitor's own e-mail address in order to subscribe them, so it collects information about the user. Neither the snapshot nor the live HTML has an autocomplete attribute on the input or its Mailchimp form. The Understanding document for 1.3.5 says type="email" does not identify whether the address is the user's own, and H98 (autocomplete="email") is the means of doing so. I found no technique that makes the field pass. I could not check the message's remark about Chromium's form check, but it does not change the verdict.

subject: Pimoroni
message: The link text "Pimoroni" is shared by 2 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.

patch.after: Pimoroni Products

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 'Pimoroni' link in the header's department navigation, between 'Pico' and 'Adafruit'. It leads to /collections/pimoroni, whose heading is 'Pimoroni' (Pimoroni's own products), so its text names its destination the same way its brand siblings do. The other link named "Pimoroni" is the logo, which leads home and carries the accessible description 'Back to the home page'; it is not in the department navigation. Understanding 2.4.4 calls different text for different destinations a best practice. ACT rule fd3a94 covers only links that share a programmatically determined context, which these two do not, and the general rule for identical names maps to 2.4.9 (AAA). 2.4.4 is met.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The link 'Pimoroni' sits in the header's department navigation (Raspberry Pi, Pico, Pimoroni, Adafruit, Breakouts...) and goes to /collections/pimoroni. That page is titled 'Pimoroni Products' and its heading is 'Pimoroni'. The other link with the same name is the logo link to the home page, which also carries the description 'Back to the home page'. This link's text names its destination, just as its sibling brand link 'Adafruit' does, so its purpose can be determined. The Understanding document for 2.4.4 calls different text for different destinations a best practice, not a requirement, so the shared name alone is not a failure of 2.4.4.

ref: #content > footer > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > picture > img
subject: american-express
message: The text alternative "american-express" repeats the image's file name: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the American Express logo in the footer's row of accepted payment methods, with alt="american-express" (live page unchanged). The file name happens to be the brand name, so the alt text gives the same information the logo does: American Express is accepted. A screen reader reads it as "american express", and the neighbouring logos (visa, mastercard, paypal, klarna) work the same way. F30 covers text alternatives that are not alternatives, such as "image" or "spacer.gif", and this one is a real alternative. The rule flagged it only because the alt matches the file name, which is stricter than 1.1.1 requires.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the American Express logo in the footer's row of accepted payment methods (the screenshot crop shows the blue AmEx mark). Its alt, "american-express", matches the file name american-express.png, but that name is itself an accurate alternative: it identifies the brand, as the sibling alts "visa", "mastercard", "paypal" and "klarna" do. F30 only covers file names that are not valid text alternatives in their own right ("Oct.jpg", "Chart.jpg"), and screen readers do not normally speak the hyphen. The rule treats any match with the file name as a failure, which is stricter than 1.1.1.

message: The field "Email address" asks for the user's email address, but autocomplete="off" does not identify that purpose.

patch.before: <input class="css-cpt18j" id="newsletter" name="newsletter" type="email" data-testid="input-form-input" data-clearable="false" data-loading="false" autocomplete="off" aria-invalid="false" placeholder="Email address" data-has-value="false" aria-disabled="false" value="">
patch.after: <input class="css-cpt18j" id="newsletter" name="newsletter" type="email" data-testid="input-form-input" data-clearable="false" data-loading="false" autocomplete="email" aria-invalid="false" placeholder="Email address" data-has-value="false" aria-disabled="false" value="">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the footer newsletter sign-up field (input#newsletter, type=email, with a visually hidden label "Email address"). It asks for the user's own email address, which is the 'email' purpose in the Input Purposes list, so 1.3.5 applies. It has autocomplete="off" in both the snapshot and the live page loaded in Edge, so no autocomplete token identifies its purpose. type="email" only describes the data format: it does not say whose email it is, and it is not the H98 technique. The purpose is therefore not programmatically identified, and this fails 1.3.5 as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the footer newsletter sign-up field (input type=email, id=newsletter, sr-only label "Email address", next to a "Sign up" button). It asks for the user's own email address, which is an Input Purpose (email), and it carries autocomplete="off". Nothing else on the field (no ARIA, no microdata) declares its purpose. The 1.3.5 Understanding document says type="email" does not establish that the field is the user's email, and that input purposes must still be programmatically determinable when authors turn autofill off. I found no technique that makes it pass, so the finding holds.

ref: #main > div:nth-of-type(1) > section > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > nav > button
subject: Expand breadcrumb navigation
message: The icon of this button ("Expand breadcrumb navigation") has at most 2.65:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ff9718 on #666666). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
html: <button class="css-1lbpys4" aria-label="Expand breadcrumb navigation" data-testid="breadcrumb-desktop-toggle" type="button">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the 40x40 'Expand breadcrumb navigation' button in the hero. It shows only an orange chevron icon and has no border or fill of its own. It sits inside the breadcrumb pill, whose computed background (live) is solid rgb(102,102,102). In the screenshot the chevron's pixels are #ff9718 and the surrounding pixels are uniform #666666, which gives 2.65:1. The live page computes the same colours. The chevron is the only visual cue that this control exists and what it does, so as an icon it needs 3:1 against adjacent colours under 1.4.11 (G207), and it falls short.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the icon-only 'Expand breadcrumb navigation' toggle at the left of the breadcrumb pill over the hero image. I sampled the screenshot inside the button's 40x40 bounds: the chevron's solid pixels are #ff9718 and its surround is a uniform #666666, which gives 2.65:1, so the rule measured correctly. The button has no text and no boundary of its own (the pill's white outline wraps the whole breadcrumb, not the control), so the chevron is the only visual sign that the control exists and what it does. The 1.4.11 Understanding document treats such arrow symbols as graphical objects that need 3:1. I could not re-check the live page, which returned HTTP 403 to curl.

subject: searchbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a searchbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "searchbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <input class="search-suggestions-search-input css-1bvetc4" id="search-suggestions" name="search-suggestions" type="search" data-testid="search-suggestions-input-input" data-clearable="true" data-loading="false" autocomplete="off" aria-invalid="false" placeholder="Search product or services" data-has-value="false" aria-disabled="false" value="">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the header search field (input#search-suggestions, type=search). It is tied to <label for="search-suggestions" class="sr-only"></label>, and that label is empty in both the snapshot and the live page. The CDP data in the snapshot shows the searchbox labelled by that label, with no name. I loaded the live page in headless Edge 155 and the searchbox's computed name is "". A minimal test in the same engine confirms that an empty associated label wins over the placeholder (the placeholder source is marked superseded). So in Chromium browsers the field has no accessible name, and the placeholder 'Search product or services' is exposed only as a placeholder. Some screen readers may still voice that placeholder and Firefox may use it as the name, but in the main engine the name cannot be programmatically determined, so the 4.1.2 claim holds.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the header search input (type=search, placeholder "Search product or services"). It is associated with an sr-only <label for=search-suggestions> that is empty. The CDP tree in the snapshot gives it no name and no nameFrom, so in Chrome the finding is factually right. However, HTML-AAM 4.1.1 says that when the label yields nothing, the title and then the placeholder become the name. ACT rule e086e5 passes a placeholder-only field (Passed Example 5), and browsers expose the placeholder separately, where NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver and TalkBack usually announce it, so users likely hear more than 'searchbox'. Under the spec the field has a name; in the dominant browser it does not. Competent auditors would reasonably split on whether that is a 4.1.2 failure. The empty label is plainly an authoring defect either way. I could not re-check the live page, which returned HTTP 403.

subject: Gray gradient
message: The text alternative "Gray gradient" names an image that is decorative.

patch.ref: html > body > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > section > div:nth-of-type(2) > img:nth-of-type(2)

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is a 32px gradient SVG (data-identity 'single-line-nav-fade-right') laid over the edge of the horizontally scrolling utility nav at the top of the header, a purely visual fade with no information. The snapshot's CDP tree exposes it as role image with name 'Gray gradient' from its alt, no role=presentation and no aria-hidden ancestor, and the live HTML still carries alt="Gray gradient". A decorative image that is not implemented so AT can ignore it fails 1.1.1 (documented failure F38: decorative img with non-null alt and no presentation role); screen readers announce 'Gray gradient, image' inside the nav. Should be alt="". This one sits at the right edge of the Locations list.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: A purely presentational fade overlay (data-identity='single-line-nav-fade-right', a 32x40 gray gradient SVG) at the edge of the header's utility bar; the screenshot shows it only softens the bar's edge and conveys no information. I looked for a reason it would pass: no aria-hidden or role=presentation on it or its ancestors, and the browser's accessibility tree exposes it as an image named 'Gray gradient' (nameFrom alt). The live page still has alt='Gray gradient'. A decorative image with a non-null alt that screen readers announce is documented failure F39 (and F38), so the claim holds.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 144px header icon (three pink-and-white blood cells on a navy disc) above 'About Cancer' and the H1 'Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL)'. subject: WhatsApp
message: The icon of this link ("WhatsApp") has at most 1.98:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#25d366 on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the header link 'WhatsApp' (aria-label WhatsApp). Its only content is the WhatsApp logo: a disc in WhatsApp's brand green #25D366 with a white glyph, shown with the other social logos in their own brand colours (screenshot). The measured contrast of about 1.98:1 is real. However, the Understanding document for 1.4.11 exempts logos under the essential exception ('the brand logo of an organization or product... is generally presented in the brand's specific colors; it is therefore exempt'). It also states that this exemption normatively carries over to a user interface component whose only visible content is the logo. The low contrast comes from WhatsApp's own brand colour, not from an author choice to dim a logo that normally contrasts, so the carve-out for author choice does not apply. Recommending a higher-contrast variant is a best practice; this is not a 1.4.11 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the icon-only WhatsApp channel link in the site header. Its SVG ('whatsapp-negative' in the site sprite) is the WhatsApp mark drawn as a brand-green #25d366 disc with the glyph knocked out, on the white header, and the measured 1.98:1 is correct. However, the 1.4.11 Understanding document treats brand logos shown in the brand's own colours as exempt under the essential exception. For a logo that is the only visible content of a control, it only advises that authors 'may choose' a higher-contrast variant or 'should consider' adding an element; it does not require one. WhatsApp's own green is inherently about 2:1 on white, so this is not an author-chosen low-contrast presentation. Requiring 3:1 here is stricter than WCAG as its Understanding document reads.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: 'Leia Mais' is Taboola's article expander, a[href=#] in div.tbl-read-more-box inside article#digital. The article is visibly clipped: it has class tbl-forkorts-article-active, and its box is 765px tall while the content is 3353px. The button sits at the cut-off in the screenshot. It does not navigate; it reveals the rest of the article. So 'does not tell where the link goes' misreads it, and sighted users get its purpose from the truncated text just above. Programmatically, though, its only context is the enclosing article, not a sentence, paragraph or list item. Screen reader users, for whom the text was never hidden, meet a bare 'Leia Mais' after the tags. Competent auditors would split between passing it (a single 'read more' within the article it expands) and failing 2.4.4. The clearer defect is 4.1.2: a link used as a disclosure button with no expanded state.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is Taboola's 'Leia Mais' control: an a href="#" in div.tbl-read-more-box inside the article, which carries the class tbl-forkorts-article. The article is clipped to a short preview: its box ends near y=1441, while its text runs on for about 3,300 px. This button sits at the cut-off, just below the lead photo and caption, as the screenshot shows, and activating it expands the same article. It does not navigate anywhere. auditor.rationale: This is the visible desktop footer logo: an img with alt="Logo" that is the only content of a link to "/", so the link's computed name is "Logo". The image shows the brand wordmark "fleury" with the "100 anos" mark. "Logo" names the kind of image, not its content, in the same way as the "image" and "picture" examples in F30. It does not say whose logo it is or that the link goes to the home page, which 1.1.1 requires for a control. The header logo (alt "Fleury") and the hidden mobile footer (alt "Logo da Fleury") show the authors could do this properly. The live page still has alt="Logo" on this image.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the Fleury logo image (the word 'fleury' and the '100 anos' mark). It is the only content of the visible desktop footer's link to the home page (/). The link has no aria-label, title or hidden text, so its accessible name is just 'Logo' (snapshot: name from contents). I looked for a reason it could pass and found none. The image is functional, so it cannot be decorative. 'Logo' is neither the brand name nor the destination; it is a generic word of the same kind as F30's 'image' or 'picture'. Putting 'Logo' in place of the image loses both the information (Fleury) and the function (go to the home page), which is F30's test, so 1.1.1 fails. The finding's 'file name or a placeholder' holds on the placeholder side. The hidden mobile footer uses alt 'Logo da Fleury', which does not help the visible one, and the live page still serves alt='Logo' in this footer.

message: The text alternative "App Store Badge" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the App Store badge image (it reads "Baixar em App Store") that is the only content of a link to the Fleury Pacientes app on apps.apple.com. It sits next to the Google Play badge, under the visible text "Aplicativos Fleury". Its alt, "App Store Badge", does name the destination (the App Store) and tells it apart from the Google Play link. The image itself names no app, so the alternative carries about the same information and serves the same purpose. The extra word "Badge" and the missing "Baixar em" make the alt worse than "Baixar na App Store", but that is a wording problem, not a 1.1.1 failure. The claim that it does not say where the link leads does not hold, and the checker had the href and the surrounding text.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'Baixar em App Store' badge. It is the only content of a footer link to the Fleury Pacientes app on apps.apple.com, and it sits under the visible text 'Aplicativos Fleury'. The finding says its alt does not say where the link leads, but 'App Store Badge' does name the destination: the App Store. The image itself shows only 'Baixar em' and 'App Store', with no app name, so the alternative carries the image's essential information and its function (a link to the App Store). It could replace the image without loss, which is what 1.1.1 and F30's test ask. The extra word 'Badge', the dropped 'Baixar em' and the English wording on a pt-BR page are quality issues, not a 1.1.1 failure. Whether the link's purpose is clear without naming the app is a 2.4.4 question, not this criterion's ('Aplicativos Fleury' is a sibling paragraph, not a heading or the enclosing paragraph). The model had the alt, the crop and the href and misjudged them. The live page still has this alt.

subject: Política de Cookies
message: The text "Política de Cookies" has at most 4.31:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ed0f69 on #ffffff), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (an element over or under it). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <a class="ot-cookie-policy-link" href="https://privacyportal.onetrust.com/policies/4b90a165-da16-4729-ae7d-a1ada2835ea8?context=eyJkc1BvcnRhbElkIjoiMGFjZGE4ODgtNDNlZS00OTdjLTk4MmQtMTExMmE2Y2ZhM2NkIn0=" aria-label="Mais informação sobre a sua privacidade, abre num separador novo" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the "Política de Cookies" link in the OneTrust cookie banner, which is visible when the page loads. The snapshot records its CSS colour as #ed0f69 on the banner's #ffffff background, at 13px bold. I sampled the screenshot pixels and the glyphs are #ed0f69 on pure white, which gives 4.31:1. 13px bold is well under the large-text threshold (14pt bold, about 18.7px), so 4.5:1 applies and the link fails. None of the exceptions (incidental text, logotype) apply. The live OneTrust configuration that GTM loads on www.fleury.com.br (domain script 0191d62a) still sets BannerLinksTextColor #ed0f69 on BackgroundColor #FFFFFF.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'Política de Cookies' link in the OneTrust cookie banner. It is 13px bold, which is normal-size text, so it needs 4.5:1. The snapshot took the colour #ed0f69 from CSS and found white behind the text. I measured the page screenshot myself: the solid core of the glyphs and of the underline is exactly #ed0f69 on #ffffff, which is 4.31:1. So the colour is not an anti-aliasing artefact or a banner caught fading in, and the dark overlay lies behind the banner, not over it. I looked for an exemption and found none: the link is active and visible, it is not a logotype, the Understanding document says brand colours are not exempt, and the page has no contrast switcher. The banner is third-party, but it is content on this page, in colours the site configured. It fails 1.4.3 as reported. I did not re-check the banner's styling on the live page.
