That gives rgba(10,10,10,0.5). The text pixels in the screenshot are #848484 on #ffffff, which is 3.74:1, below 4.5:1. The Understanding document for 1.4.3 says the criterion applies to placeholder text. The field is active, so no incidental-text exception applies, and I found no contrast switcher on the page. It fails 1.4.3 as reported, and the live page still has the same field and CSS.

evidence: Tab ×1: <a> focused and blurred; 740 px of its indicator around it: #cfcfcf (732 px) next to #ffffff (100%): 1.56:1

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header logo link (img alt 'Fleury', href '/'). On the live page (2026-10-23, 1280x800, after dismissing the cookie banner) its computed focus style is 'outline: auto 1px' with an author-set outline-color of oklab(0.708 / 0.5) (the site's global 'outline-ring/50'), which renders as a thin #cfcfcf ring on the white header. Comparing the focused and blurred pixels, that ring (about 740 px) is the only change, and #cfcfcf against #ffffff is 1.56:1. Because the author changed the indicator's color, the user-agent exception does not apply, and per the 1.4.11 Understanding (Figure 43) an author-styled focus indicator needs 3:1 against adjacent colors. This fails as reported.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Header logo link (img alt Fleury). I looked for reasons the finding could be wrong. In headless Edge on the live page at 1280x800, with the cookie banner dismissed, focusing it shows outline: auto in oklab(0.708 0 0 / 0.5), i.e. #a1a1a1 at 50%. That colour comes from the site's global outline-ring/50 rule, so the author changed the focus style and the user-agent exception of 1.4.11 does not apply. The ring renders as about 2 px of #cfcfcf on white: 1.56:1. Comparing focused and blurred pixels, the ring is the only change: no background, text or underline cue. The probe's measurement matches the live page, and the Understanding for 1.4.11 says the focus indicator must have 3:1 against the adjacent background, so I found no reason that holds up.

evidence: Tab ×9 in a 390×844 window: <a> "FoundationOne®: como o perfil genômico abrangente contribui…" at y 622; 25 of 25 grid points hit <div> "Bandeira de biscoitos" #onetrust-banner-sdk (position: fixed, 375×392 px at y 548); painting it changed 0 px and hiding it 0 px; scroll-padding-bottom: 392px on html would keep focused elements clear of it
html: FoundationOne®: como o perfil genômico abrangente contribui para a personalização do tratamento do câncer

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The 'FoundationOne®...' sidebar link at 390x844, reported as entirely hidden behind the OneTrust cookie banner. The probe's own record shows a race on load. The walk began about 3.9 s after load, before the banner appeared. At Tab 9 the banner was still sliding in: the recorded banner y of 548 is mid-animation, and its resting y is 452. On the very next step, focus was inside the banner, and the walk then reports a focus trap in the banner. I reproduced this live. Tabbing right after load, the link is first fully visible. The banner then slides over it for under a second, after which OneTrust moves focus onto the banner. With the banner showing, Tab, Shift+Tab and ArrowDown then Tab all keep focus inside the banner, behind a dark page filter, and Escape closes it. Per the 2.4.11 Understanding, making the banner modal so the user must dismiss it before navigating the page is a way to pass. A keyboard user is never left with focus on a hidden page element: the moment caught here is a brief animation race, after which focus goes to visible banner controls. The rule had this trap data in the same walk and still reported a failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: FoundationOne link in the sidebar; the finding says that at 390x844 it is fully hidden behind the OneTrust cookie banner when focused. The snapshot's own walk record shows that this walk did not wait for idle (idleMs 0). It reached the link at Tab x9, about 4.35 s after load and 35 to 100 ms per key. One step later, focus was inside the banner and stayed trapped there. I drove the live page in headless Edge at 390x844. The banner comes with a full-viewport 50% black overlay that blocks the page. About 0.8 s after it appears it takes focus. After that, Tab, Shift+Tab and ArrowDown then Tab all cycle inside its four controls, and Escape dismisses it. In its settled state the banner is effectively modal, which the Understanding for 2.4.11 lists as a way to pass ('making the banner modal so the user has to dismiss the banner before navigating through the page'). A keyboard user cannot move focus to the link while the banner is up, and once it is dismissed nothing covers the link. The probe caught a transient state during load, before the banner took focus, so the claim does not hold for the page as users meet it. The page may have changed since the run, but the snapshot's own trap record shows the same banner trap then.

patch.to: Alerta de segurança: Evite golpes. O Hcor não faz ligações para solicitar pagamentos antecipados.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the active (not cloned) slide of the home-page Owl carousel: an unlinked banner image with alt "Alerta de Golpe" (scam alert). The crop Rampa used shows a banner whose own text reads "Alerta de segurança: Evite golpes.", with a warning icon and the sentence that Hcor does not phone to ask for advance payments for medicines, treatment changes or inpatient procedures. The alt names exactly what the image shows, so the claim that it describes something the image does not show is wrong. The alt is arguably incomplete, because it leaves out the warning sentence (the header's text bar "AVISO – GOLPE" gives a similar but not identical notice). That would be a different 1.1.1 claim, about the alt not carrying the same information, not the one reported. The live markup is unchanged.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the image on the 'Alerta de Golpe' hero carousel slide. It is the active owl-item, not a clone, and not inside a link. The crop the model saw shows a banner reading 'Alerta de segurança: Evite golpes.', an exclamation-mark bubble, and a warning that Hcor does not phone patients to ask for advance payments. The site header and the quick-access cards overlap the crop, but the banner is plainly visible. 'Alerta de Golpe' (scam alert) names exactly what the image shows, so the claim that the alternative describes something the image does not show is wrong. An auditor might separately find the alt too short for an image of text, since it leaves out the warning sentence (the page's top bar carries a similar warning as real text), but that is a different claim from the one reported.

subject: Oncologia
message: The text "Oncologia" has at most 2.83:1 contrast with what is behind it (#51ab74 on #ffffff), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a pseudo-element). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the "Oncologia" category link pill on the first, visible "Hcor explica" card. The live CSS has .card .category {background:#FFF; font-size:12px; font-weight:600} and .ctx-green .card .category {color:#51AB74}. I sampled the screenshot and found #51ab74 glyph pixels on #ffffff, a ratio of 2.83:1. At 12px and weight 600 it is not large text, so 4.5:1 applies. It is an active link, neither incidental nor a logotype, so it fails 1.4.3.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'Oncologia' category link (12px, weight 600) on the white pill over the image of the first 'Hcor explica' card. The live stylesheet confirms the colours: .card .category sets a #FFF background at 12px/600, and .ctx-green .card .category sets the text to #51AB74. The screenshot pixels show #51ab74 glyphs on #ffffff. That is 2.83:1, below the 4.5:1 that text needs when it is not large. It is visible, active text, not incidental and not a logotype. The page has no contrast toggle (G174) and no other alternative version, so the finding is a real 1.4.3 failure.

ref: html > body > main > section > section:nth-of-type(3) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > button:nth-of-type(1)
message: When this element has keyboard focus, its focus indicator (#e9f2ec, inside it) has a contrast of 1.00:1 at most with the colors next to it, under the 3:1 that WCAG 1.4.11 asks of visual information needed to identify a state. Give the indicator a color with at least 3:1 against what surrounds it, such as an outline of 2 px that is dark on a light page.
evidence: Tab ×75: <button> "‹" focused and blurred; 226 px of its indicator inside it: #e9f2ec (190 px) next to #e9f2ec (100%): 1.00:1

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: I drove the live page in headless Edge at 1280x800 and tabbed to this owl-carousel arrow in the 'Hcor explica' section. The site removes the outline (computed outline: none) and the only focus cue is the rule '.carousel .owl-prev/.owl-next:focus {transform: scale(1.08)}': the pale #e9f2ec button grows by about 1.5 px a side on a white section, about 1.13:1, and its green chevron is about 2.5:1 against the button. Nothing that marks the focused state reaches 3:1, so the indicator fails 1.4.11 (F78 lists 1.4.11 for styling that leaves the focus indicator effectively invisible). The owl 'disabled' class on the prev button is not exposed or styled as inactive, and the button stays in the tab order, so the inactive exception does not apply. Rampa's 'next to #e9f2ec' is a loose way to name the neighbouring colour, but the conclusion holds.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: Owl-carousel 'previous' button of the Hcor explica carousel (class owl-prev disabled: clicking it does nothing at the first slide, but it stays focusable and looks active). On the live page (headless Edge, 1280x800) the only change on keyboard focus is transform: scale(1.08); outline stays none and no colour changes. The reported indicator, #e9f2ec next to #e9f2ec at 1.00:1, is an artefact. Those are pixels inside the button that changed only because the arrow glyph moved when it scaled, not an indicator. Measured properly, the enlarged pale band is #e9f2ec on white (about 1.14:1) and the arrow is #64b483 on #e9f2ec (2.19:1). The button is also functionally inactive, and 1.4.11 exempts inactive components. Whether a size change alone is a focus indicator that 1.4.11 measures is contested: the Understanding document says 1.4.11 does not directly compare the focused and unfocused states of a control, while a strict reading treats the enlarged band as an indicator outside the component that must reach 3:1 with the background. Competent auditors would disagree, so neither label is safe.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the footer phone button '(11) 3053-6611'. On the live page its focus outline is removed (outline: none), and the only change on focus is '.button-default:focus {opacity: .95}', which moves the button from #6ac0d5 to about #66bad0 on the dark footer. The Understanding document for 1.4.11 says a change of colour within the component is not in scope of non-text contrast (Figure 15), and the focused button keeps its contrast with the dark footer. message: Pressing "I" with focus on the page, and no other key held, changes it: single character key shortcuts that work while no control has focus. Nothing on this page turns them off or remaps them. Let people turn them off, or remap them to include a key such as Ctrl or Alt, or make each work only while its control has focus (WCAG 2.1.4; F99). If a setting elsewhere, such as another page or the account settings, already does this, the criterion is satisfied: waive this finding (rampa waive).
evidence: "I" changed what the window shows; each on two presses with focus on the body, and nothing changed in the same wait with no key

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The claim is that pressing 'I' with focus on the body changes the page. I listed the live page's key listeners over CDP: there are only Bootstrap's delegated dropdown keydown/keyup handlers and a jQuery body keyup that reacts to Esc (keyCode 27). Nothing handles 'I'. In repeated trials, screen changes came at random with 'I', 'i', Shift+I and other letters alike. They match the hero carousel's autoplay (the region 13,151 to 1267,714) and the animated WhatsApp popup, not the key press. The probe credited an autoplay change to the key. There is no single-character shortcut, so 2.1.4 does not fail.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The finding says pressing 'I' with focus on the body changes the page. I replayed it on the live page at 1280x800 and 320x256 with a listener on keydown, keypress and keyup. 'I', 'i' and Shift+I reach the body unhandled (defaultPrevented false), scroll does not move, and repeated presses changed 0 px. When pixels did change, they changed equally on no-key control waits and on other letters: the hero carousel autoplay, the animated floating 'Faça seu agendamento' button and the top banner region. The only document key listeners come from Bootstrap's delegated handlers and the theme's Escape handler for the mobile side nav. No single-character shortcut exists, so the probe attributed a periodic animation to the key press.

subject: Passados-imaginados.jpg
message: The text alternative "Passados-imaginados.jpg" is a file name: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The image has alt="Passados-imaginados.jpg" and the caption 'PASSADOS IMAGINADOS'. It is one of the eleven photos in the 'Conheça nossas novas exposições' auto-scrolling media wheel (premium-adv-carousel, not a link), followed by a plain caption span. The alt is the upload's file name with its extension, the snapshot's AX tree exposes the image with that name (nameFrom alt), and the live page (curl, 2026-10-23) still serves the same alt. I opened the image itself: it is a photograph of visitors standing around the large city model, with projected questions on the walls. The file name does not describe that picture, so it is not a text alternative (F30: file names used as text alternatives); and if the photo were treated as decorative beside its caption, a non-null alt would still fail (F39), because the image is not ignorable by assistive technology. Either way 1.1.1 fails as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is a carousel image in 'Conheça nossas novas exposições' with alt="Passados-imaginados.jpg", the exact file name in its src. In the Chromium accessibility tree it is exposed as an image named from the alt (not ignored, no aria-hidden, not inside a link or a named ancestor), and the live page's server HTML still has the same alt. I opened the image file: it is a photograph, showing visitors around a city model, with questions projected on the walls, not a picture of the words in the file name. The alt is the exhibition title from the visible caption (PASSADOS IMAGINADOS) with file-name residue (hyphens and .jpg), so it does not describe the image, and the image is not marked as decorative either (alt is not empty). F30 names file names that are not valid alternatives in their own right, ACT rule 9eb3f6 fails a file name with its extension even when the stem matches the subject, and F39 fails a non-null alt on an image that should be ignored, so the image fails whether it is informative or decorative. The image being off-screen at capture time (the widget is an infinite marquee) does not matter: it scrolls into view and screen readers read it anyway. I found no technique that makes it pass.

message: The text alternative "min_coletar-Imagens-e-objetos.jpg" is a file name: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The image has alt="min_coletar-Imagens-e-objetos.jpg" and the caption 'COLETAR: IMAGENS E OBJETOS'. It is one of the eleven photos in the 'Conheça nossas novas exposições' auto-scrolling media wheel (premium-adv-carousel, not a link), followed by a plain caption span. The alt is the upload's file name with its extension, the snapshot's AX tree exposes the image with that name (nameFrom alt), and the live page (curl, 2026-10-23) still serves the same alt. I opened the image itself: it is a photograph of a visitor in front of a wall of framed portrait paintings. The file name does not describe that picture, so it is not a text alternative (F30: file names used as text alternatives); and if the photo were treated as decorative beside its caption, a non-null alt would still fail (F39), because the image is not ignorable by assistive technology. Either way 1.1.1 fails as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is a carousel image in 'Conheça nossas novas exposições' with alt="min_coletar-Imagens-e-objetos.jpg", the exact file name in its src. In the Chromium accessibility tree it is exposed as an image named from the alt (not ignored, no aria-hidden, not inside a link or a named ancestor), and the live page's server HTML still has the same alt. I opened the image file: it is a photograph, showing a visitor in front of a wall of framed portraits, not a picture of the words in the file name. The alt is the exhibition title from the visible caption (COLETAR: IMAGENS E OBJETOS) with file-name residue (a 'min_' prefix, hyphens and .jpg), so it does not describe the image, and the image is not marked as decorative either (alt is not empty). F30 names file names that are not valid alternatives in their own right, ACT rule 9eb3f6 fails a file name with its extension even when the stem matches the subject, and F39 fails a non-null alt on an image that should be ignored, so the image fails whether it is informative or decorative. The image being off-screen at capture time (the widget is an infinite marquee) does not matter: it scrolls into view and screen readers read it anyway. I found no technique that makes it pass.

subject: logo-museu
message: The text alternative "logo-museu" is a file name or a placeholder.

patch.ref: #masthead > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div > a > div > div > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header logo is an image of the text 'MUSEU DO IPIRANGA — USP' (crop and screenshot) and is the only content of the link to the home page; its alt 'logo-museu' is the stem of its file name logo-museu.png, still the same on the live page. The AX tree gives the link the name 'logo-museu' (nameFrom contents); the other 'Museu do Ipiranga' home link in the masthead is hidden (bhf-hidden), so nothing else names it. 'logo-museu' leaves out the museum's name and USP, the text the image shows, and does not say where the link goes, so it is a file-name placeholder rather than an equivalent (F30). 1.1.1 fails as reported; the same name also weakens the link's purpose under 2.4.4.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the header logo, the only content of the link to the home page. Its alt 'logo-museu' is the file name logo-museu.png without the extension. The crop and the screenshot show a picture of the words 'MUSEU DO IPIRANGA — USP'. In the Chromium accessibility tree, the link is named 'logo-museu' from its contents. The site-title link 'Museu do Ipiranga' (p.main-title.bhf-hidden) is display:none and not in the tree, and the live markup has no aria-label or title on the link. 'logo-museu' ('museum logo') leaves out the museum's name and the USP text, and it does not say where the link goes, so it does not serve the same purpose (F30). The finding's claim (a file name or placeholder) holds. The same name also weakens link purpose (2.4.4).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the footer newsletter sign-up's name field (type=text, name="name", placeholder 'Digite seu Nome', required). It collects the user's own name, a purpose in the WCAG input-purpose list, and HTML supports autocomplete, but the rendered input has no autocomplete attribute. The live page builds the field with the iSend forms script, whose text-field builder sets only type, id, name, placeholder, maxlength, class and required, so this is still true. The name attribute is not a programmatic purpose (H98 needs autocomplete), and the snapshot records Chromium's FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError for this input, which backs the message. 1.3.5 fails (autocomplete="name", or given-name, would be needed).

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the footer newsletter's 'Digite seu Nome' field, injected by the iSend widget: input type=text name=name, named only by its placeholder, with no autocomplete attribute and no form element around it. It asks for the visitor's own name, a purpose in the 1.3.5 list ('name'). The Understanding document says heuristics such as the name attribute are not enough: the purpose must be exposed through the autocomplete attribute (H98). The snapshot records Chromium's FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError issue on this field, which confirms the side claim. The live iSend script creates its inputs without ever setting autocomplete, so the field still fails today. Whether the right token is name or given-name, no purpose is identified.

message: The keyboard walk never reached this control with Tab or Shift+Tab: someone who uses a keyboard cannot operate it.
evidence: Tab ×80 forward and Shift+Tab ×80 backward reached 79 element(s), never <iframe> "Museu do Ipiranga: bem-vindo a uma nova história. (30s)"; it is a native control that never took focus

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the Elementor background-video iframe (YouTube embed, controls=0, role=presentation) behind the hero. Live, the iframe and its .elementor-background-video-container have pointer-events: none, so mouse users cannot operate anything in it either. It has no controls and offers no function, so 2.1.1 has nothing to require keyboard access for. The rule treated a decorative frame as a 'native control'. An autoplaying 30 s video with no pause control may be a 2.2.2 issue, but that is not what this finding claims.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the Elementor hero background video: a YouTube iframe (controls=0, role=presentation) inside div.elementor-background-video-container. On the live page both the iframe and that container have pointer-events: none, so a mouse user cannot interact with it either; there is no functionality here that only a pointer can reach, which is what 2.1.1 is about (a missing pause control would be a 2.2.2 question, not this one). The 'never reached' claim also does not hold: in my own headless Edge Tab walk at 1280x800 focus entered the iframe twice (YouTube's caption window and its 'Mostrar controles do player' button). The probe's network guard blocked YouTube's player requests (youtubei/v1/player) and its screenshot shows a blank hero, so the frame had nothing focusable in the probe run: an artefact of the probe environment.

message: When this element receives keyboard focus, no pixel changes, in its box or anywhere in the viewport: there is no visible focus indicator.
evidence: Tab ×13: <a> focused and blurred; 0 px changed in the 372×191 px around the element, 0 px in the 1024000 px of the viewport (captured twice)

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header logo link (an inline <a> wrapping the block-level logo image, 330x126 at 10,55). Checked live in headless Edge with the welcome modal closed: reaching the link with a real Tab gives :focus-visible and a computed 3px outline, but the outline is drawn on the empty inline fragments. 0 px of the header region changed between focused and unfocused. The probe also recorded 0 px changed. No other element on the page shows focus for it, so this keyboard-operable link has no visible focus indicator: 2.4.7 fails.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The header logo link (a.elementor-clickable wrapping the logo image, href to the home page). I looked for a reason it could pass: the site CSS gives it outline: 3px solid black on focus, but the anchor is display: inline around block children, so the outline is not painted. With the welcome modal removed from the live page, Tab-focusing versus blurring the logo changed 0 px within 20 px of it, and a screenshot of it focused shows no ring, underline or other change. This is not caused by the modal (it fails without it), and the accessibility toolbar offers no focus-highlight mode, so no mode of operation shows its focus: 2.4.7 fails.

message: When this element receives keyboard focus, no pixel changes, in its box or anywhere in the viewport: there is no visible focus indicator.
evidence: Tab ×15: <div> "O Museu" focused and blurred; 0 px changed in the 181×118 px around the element, 0 px in the 1024000 px of the viewport (captured twice); the element is entirely under #premium-modal-cbfd80b (see 2.4.11), so an indicator it has cannot show

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 'O Museu' submenu container (div role=button, tabindex 0) in the main nav at 369,87 in a 1280x800 window. The welcome modal (#premium-modal-cbfd80b, 'Bem vindo ao museu') opens by itself a few seconds after load, does not take or contain focus (activeElement stays on body, Tab goes to the page behind it, Escape only works with focus inside it), and its white dialog box is opaque (rgb(255,255,255), 700x650 at x 290-990, y 75-725 in a 1280x800 window; 390x694 at y 75-769 in a 390x844 window) over a semi-transparent rgba(0,0,0,.5) backdrop. Live in headless Edge with the modal open, focusing this element changed 0 px in its area because it sits entirely under the opaque dialog box; with the modal closed the same element shows a black outline focus indicator (it is not missing in the CSS). So the cause is obscuring, not missing styling, but the finding names that cause, and the 2.4.11 Understanding says a fully obscured focus indicator would likely fail 2.4.7 as well; in the state a keyboard user meets on load no indicator is visible.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The 'O Museu' submenu toggle (div.hfe-has-submenu-container, role=button) in the main menu. When Rampa tabbed to it, the welcome popup (#premium-modal-cbfd80b, a Premium Addons modal that opens by itself on page load and does not take or trap focus) was lying over it. The 0 px change comes from the popup's opaque white panel (290-990 x 75-725 px at 1280x800) covering the element, as the finding's own evidence says. With the popup removed on the live page, focusing it produces a visible black outline (2px solid, about 720 px changed around it; confirmed in a screenshot), so a mode where the indicator is visible exists and 2.4.7 is met. Hiding the focused element behind author content is the 2.4.11 failure, reported separately for the same elements; reporting it again under 2.4.7 applies the wrong criterion.

evidence: Tab ×18: <a> "African American Civil War MemorialMemorialDistrict of Colu…" focused and blurred; 6474 px of its indicator around it: #2491ff (5922 px) next to #f6f6f6 (57%): 2.96:1; style sheet: outline-color #2491ff, box-shadow #00000033

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 'African American Civil War Memorial' result card (a link). I re-ran a Tab walk on the live page (2026-10-23, Edge headless, 1280x800). When focused, this result card moves up a few pixels and gets a 4 px #2491ff outline with outline-offset 0. The outline sits just outside the card, on the white page that the card's box-shadow (0 3px 15px rgba(0,0,0,.2)) tints. The pixels right next to the outline on the outside are #eaeaea to #f6f6f6, which gives 2.66 to 2.96:1. Inside, it borders the photo (light sky or water at about 1.6 to 2.1:1) and, only along the bottom, the black text panel. The Understanding document says an outline drawn outside a component has to contrast with the background it sits on, and here that background is below 3:1 everywhere next to the indicator. Against plain #fff it would be 3.2:1, so the margin is small, but the colours actually rendered fail 1.4.11.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: Result card link (African American Civil War Memorial). In the live page (2026-10-23, headless Edge, Tab walk matching the probe's order) the focused card gets outline 4px solid #2491ff at offset 0, a 5 px lift and a changed box-shadow (0 3px 15px rgba(0,0,0,.2)). The card sits on a white page: pixels a little away from the card are #ffffff, and #2491ff against #ffffff is 3.20:1. The greys right next to the outline (#eaeaea to #f6f6f6, 2.66 to 2.96:1) are the card's own soft drop shadow fading to white over about 14 px. The Understanding document for 1.4.11 says that a 3D drop shadow is subsumed into the color closest to it in brightness, which here is the white background, and that an outer indicator needs to contrast with the background the component is on. Measured that way, the indicator passes 3:1, so the rule applied a stricter measurement than the criterion. The finding is marginal at best: some auditors who pick the shadow pixel would fail it.

ref: #lazy_46231 > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > img
subject: Masthead logo
message: The text alternative "Masthead logo" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: #lazy_46231 > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the homepage masthead, an image of the words "THE IRISH TIMES" (I checked the crop and the screenshot). It is not in a link and is not hidden, and its alt is "Masthead logo". That alt names what kind of image it is but not what it says, so a screen reader user hears "Masthead logo" and never the publication's name. Strictly, the image does show a masthead logo, so the finding's wording ("describes something the image does not show") is a little off. The real defect is that the alt is generic and does not convey the logo's text (alt="The Irish Times" would). If the masthead were treated as decorative, a non-empty alt would instead fail F39. Either way 1.1.1 fails. The live page still has the same alt.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The image is the page masthead, a wordmark reading "THE IRISH TIMES", with alt "Masthead logo". It is not inside a link, the page has no h1, and the small logo in the nav is aria-hidden, so this alt is how a screen reader user meets the publication name. The live page still uses it. The claim as worded, that the alt describes something the image does not show, does not hold: the image really is a masthead logo. The real 1.1.1 problem is different. The alt names the image type and leaves out the text the image shows (G94, close to F30), so it is not an equivalent. The element probably fails 1.1.1, but for a reason other than the one stated, and auditors could fairly split on whether the finding counts.

ref: #lazy_45280 > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > a
subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the live-blog timeline entry link ("1 hour ago / The storm set to hit Ireland's west coast..."). The <a> wraps an <article> that holds the time and paragraph. In the snapshot, Chrome's accessibility tree gives the link role link and name "": Chromium does not take a name from the contents of an article descendant, and the link has no aria-label or title. So when a screen reader user tabs to this focusable link, or lists the links, it is announced only as "link", and its name is not programmatically determinable in the engine the page was tested in. That fails 4.1.2, and 2.4.4 as well. Some auditors might call this a browser quirk, since AccName 1.2 recursion would include the text. But the name the platform actually exposes is empty, and the fix is trivial. The live page has changed since the run: it no longer shows the live-blog lead, so I judged from the snapshot.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is a live-blog entry link (a > article > time + p) whose visible text is "1 hour ago The storm set to hit...". The snapshot shows that Chrome's accessibility tree gives the link an empty name. This fits Chromium not taking a name from content through an <article> descendant, so the claim that the browser computes no name is accurate. Against counting it: <a><article> is valid HTML, and accname's recursive name-from-content step (2F/2H) would take the name from the text. So the empty name is a browser implementation choice, not missing author content. Name computations like axe-core's give the text, and browse-mode screen readers (NVDA, JAWS) read the link content anyway, so "announces only link" is overstated for them. Focus or API-based announcements in Chrome may still lose the name. Competent auditors would split on whether this is a 4.1.2 content failure or a user-agent quirk.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > main > div > article > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(3) > article > figure > a > img
subject: fullepisode
message: The text alternative "fullepisode" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > main > div > article > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(3) > article > figure > a > img
patch.to: A hand holding a yellow tag labeled 'ELECTION SECURITY' with a play button icon.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The image is the thumbnail of the Oct 22 full-episode card (a still of a hand holding an 'Election Security' seal). It sits inside a link to the full-episode page together with a 'Watch' play label, so the link is announced as 'Watch fullepisode'. Next to it are the visible text 'Watch the Full Episode' and a title link 'PBS NewsHour from Oct 22, 2026' to the same page. This is a functional image in a link. Its alt only needs to convey the link's purpose, or could be empty because the text around it already does. 'fullepisode' is a sloppy string taken from the file name, but it says what the thumbnail stands for, and it does not describe anything the image is not. The still itself is illustrative, not information the user needs. Replacing the image with its alt loses no function or information, so this is not the 1.1.1 failure claimed; at most it is a quality issue. The live page still has the same markup.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The image is the thumbnail inside the 'Watch' link of the 'Watch the Full Episode / PBS NewsHour from Oct 22, 2026' card. The link's accessible name is 'Watch fullepisode', and it leads to the October 22 full-episode page (title 'October 22, 2026 - PBS News Hour full episode'); the title link next to it has the same href. For an image inside a link, 1.1.1 asks the text alternative to convey the link's function, not to describe the photo (a hand holding an election-security seal). Together with 'Watch', 'fullepisode' names what the thumbnail stands for and where it leads. The alt is a run-together string taken from the file name and could be better (or empty, since the title link already covers it), but it is not false, so the claimed mismatch between alt and image is not a 1.1.1 failure. The live page is unchanged.

subject: Web ad - adjusted (1)
message: The text alternative "Web ad - adjusted (1)" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

patch.to: Join Press Pass: A new supporter program from PBS News

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The image is a Press Pass promo banner, an image of text: 'Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass. A new supporter program from PBS News. Issue my Press Pass'. It is the only content of a link to /newshour/presspass/, and the link has no other name. Its alt 'Web ad - adjusted (1)' is the media-library or file name (Web-ad-adjusted-1.png), so the link is announced as 'Web ad - adjusted (1)'. That gives neither the banner's text nor where the link leads. This is a text alternative that is not an alternative (F30), and the H30 requirement that a link-only image describe the link's function is not met, so it is a real 1.1.1 failure; it also affects 2.4.4. The live page still has the same alt.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The sidebar promo image is an image of text ('Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass. A new supporter program from PBS News. Issue my Press Pass'). It is the only content of a link to /newshour/presspass/ (title 'Press Pass | PBS News'). Its alt, and so the link's accessible name, is 'Web ad - adjusted (1)', a media-library file title. That is the F30 pattern, and it falls short of H30, which needs a linked image's alt to describe the link's function. Nothing else names the link: no aria-label, no title, and no nearby text. I found no technique that makes it pass. The live page still has this markup.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > footer > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(4) > a > img
subject: Viewers Like You
message: The text alternative "Viewers Like You" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

patch.ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > footer > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(4) > a > img

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The image is the 'Viewers Like You' logo in the footer's 'Support for News Hour Provided By' list. The other logos in the list (BNSF Railway, Consumer Cellular, Raymond James) also use the funder's name as alt. This alt reproduces the logo's text exactly. The link redirects to pbs.org/donate/ (I checked this; Rampa had not read it), and a sighted user cannot tell that from the logo either, so screen-reader users get the same information as sighted users. 1.1.1 asks for a text alternative that serves the same purpose as the image, not one that states a destination the image itself does not show. Naming the destination ('donate') is advice from the WAI tutorial, and link purpose falls under 2.4.4, whose context and 'ambiguous to users in general' provisions apply here. The checker applied a stricter rule than 1.1.1 requires.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The image is the 'VIEWERS LIKE YOU' funder logo in the footer list headed 'Support for News Hour Provided By', beside BNSF Railway, Consumer Cellular and Raymond James. Its link redirects to pbs.org/donate. The alt repeats the logo's text exactly, so it gives screen-reader users the same information the image gives sighted users and serves the same purpose (G94). Sighted users get no more destination information than 'Viewers Like You' in a funder credit either. 1.1.1 does not require an alt to state a destination the image itself does not show. Any doubt about where the link goes is shared by all users, which 2.4.4's exception for links ambiguous to users in general covers. The finding applies a stricter rule than the criterion.

It asks for the user's own email address to subscribe them to the politics newsletter, so it collects information about the user, and 'email' is one of the listed Input Purposes. The field has autocomplete="off" and no valid purpose token, so its purpose is not programmatically determinable. The 1.3.5 Understanding document says type="email" does not identify the purpose, and that purposes must stay determinable even when an author turns autofill off. H98 is not met, so this is a real 1.3.5 failure. The live HTML is unchanged.

skeptic.rationale: This is the sidebar 'Educate your inbox' newsletter field (input type=email name=email). Its only visible label is the placeholder, plus a visually hidden span. It collects the user's own email address, which is one of the listed input purposes. It has autocomplete='off' and no other purpose metadata. It also says authors who turn autofill off must still make the purpose programmatically determinable; H98 would need autocomplete='email'. I found no reason it passes. html: <input class="subscribe__input" type="email" value="" name="email" autocomplete="off" placeholder="Enter your email address">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The sidebar newsletter field shows the placeholder 'Enter your email address' as its only visible label; the label element's own text is visually hidden. The placeholder renders in the browser default #757575 at 13px, weight 400, on the field's background #f0f1f8 (the live CSS has .subscribe__box input {background-color:#f0f1f8; font-size:13px}). In the screenshot the darkest glyph pixels are #757575 on #f0f1f8, which is 4.09:1, below 4.5:1. Visible placeholder text is text, none of the 1.4.3 exceptions covers it, and here it is the only visible cue for the field. This is a real 1.4.3 failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The placeholder 'Enter your email address' is the sidebar newsletter field's only visible label. The site's ::placeholder colour rules all target other forms (.subscribe__form, .popup, .subscribe-page__topper, .footer__subscribe-form), and none of them is an ancestor of this field, which sits in .sidebar__subscribe .subscribe__box. The site only sets the placeholder's opacity to 1, so Chromium's default placeholder colour, #757575, applies. The field's background is #f0f1f8 (.subscribe__box input). That works out to 4.09:1 at 13px and weight 400, below 4.5:1. The 1.4.3 Understanding document explicitly includes placeholder text. It is a real failure.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > nav > div > div > div > button
message: When the pointer is over this control (hover), its text has a contrast of 4.35:1 at best with what is behind it, under the 4.5:1 WCAG 1.4.3 asks. Text must keep its contrast in every state a person puts it in; change the hover colors.
evidence: hover: <button> "Menu"; changed: color #ffffff → #f83036, -webkit-text-fill-color #ffffff → #f83036; #f83036 on #181c36: 4.35:1 at best, 4.35:1 at worst · 14px, 600

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The 'Menu' button in the PBS News nav bar. Live in headless Edge, hovering it changes its text from #ffffff to #f83036 (computed style, label span included). The text sits on the nav__elements background rgb(24,28,54) #181c36 and is 14px at weight 600, so it is not large text. I computed #f83036 on #181c36 at 4.35:1, under the 4.5:1 minimum. The hover state shows text a pointer user actually reads, so 1.4.3 applies, and it fails as reported.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The Menu button in the PBS News nav bar (label text 'Menu'). I checked the live page at 1280x800: on hover the label's computed color changes from #ffffff to rgb(248,48,54) (#f83036). The nav background is #181c36 (sampled from the probe screenshot), and the contrast is 4.35:1. The text is 14px at weight 600, below the large-text threshold of about 18.5px bold, so 4.5:1 applies. The Understanding document for 1.4.3 says the criterion covers text shown while a pointer hovers over an object or while it has keyboard focus. No other cue raises the contrast (the background does not change), so I found no reason the claim fails.

message: This item is marked as the current or selected one (aria-current="step"), and the only thing that shows it is an indicator (#444055, inside it) with a contrast of 1.01:1 at most with the colors next to it, under the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of visual information needed to identify a state. Give the indicator 3:1 against what surrounds it, or add a cue in the text (bold, an underline).

message: Content that appears on hover covers other content and does not close with Esc. Let people dismiss it without moving the pointer or focus, for example with Esc (WCAG 1.4.13, dismissible; SCR39).

A Tab from 'Sign in' fires focus on button.search_btn, and in the same millisecond blur on it and focus on input#search_input, while the search menu opens (aria-expanded=true). So the button's focus handler moves focus to another control without any activation. Understanding 3.2.1 lists 'focus is changed to another component when that component receives focus' as a change of context on focus, so this fails 3.2.1 as reported.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The header Search button (aria-haspopup, aria-expanded). I checked live at 1280x800: Tab from Sign in lands on #search_input, not the button, and focusing the button by script also moves focus to the input and opens the panel. Nothing is activated. The Understanding document for 3.2.1 names 'focus is changed to another component when that component receives focus' as a change of context on focus. Tabbing forward, the button can never keep focus, so the claim holds.
